item_format: Alternative Uses Task: name as many different uses as you can for a common object (e.g., a brick); scored for fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration
cognitive_process: divergent/creative ideation
engagement_affordance: 'inventor mode' brainstorm sprint with a countdown timer and pop-up idea-bubbles; rewards quantity first, then surprises with originality bonuses
adaptivity_fit: low - open-ended generation cannot be delivered as a fixed-branch CAT; needs rubric or automated originality scoring
tail_discrimination: med - originality scoring separates genuinely creative talent, but inter-rater/scoring reliability is the bottleneck at the high tail
coachability_bias_risk: scoring is subjective (low inter-rater reliability); fluency is coachable via practice; heavy verbal-expression load can penalize ELL/quiet students
advantage_vs_cogat: captures divergent/creative thinking that CogAT's convergent reasoning items ignore entirely (Renzulli creativity ring); surfaces creatively gifted students a reasoning cutoff misses
source_name: Guilford Alternative/Alternate Uses Task (public paradigm)
reuse_note: adapt_ok - classic public divergent-thinking paradigm; build local prompts and an originality scoring key

item_format: picture-prompted alternate uses for younger children: child sees a familiar object (paper plate) and says as many different uses as possible; scored for fluency and originality
cognitive_process: divergent/creative ideation
engagement_affordance: friendly on-screen character asks 'what else could this be?'; each new idea inflates a balloon; oral responses so no writing required
adaptivity_fit: low - open-ended oral generation needs human/automated scoring rather than adaptive branching
tail_discrimination: low - at ages 4-5 responses are sparse and scoring is noisy, so high-tail separation is weak
coachability_bias_risk: oral scoring is subjective; output varies with vocabulary/exposure (SES-linked); shy children under-produce, risking false negatives
advantage_vs_cogat: gives non-readers a creativity signal CogAT never collects; broadens who is flagged for talent development in early grades
source_name: Wallach-Kogan Creativity Test - Alternate Uses (public paradigm)
reuse_note: adapt_ok - Wallach-Kogan tasks are a public game-like paradigm; adapt to oral/pictorial administration for pre-readers

item_format: Instances task: 'name all the round things you can think of' (or things that make noise); scored for fluency and category flexibility
cognitive_process: divergent/associative fluency
engagement_affordance: rapid-fire 'idea machine' where each spoken answer lights up a new star; oral and untimed-feeling to reduce anxiety
adaptivity_fit: low - open generation; not CAT-compatible, requires a scoring key
tail_discrimination: low - young children's fluency overlaps heavily; weak discrimination at the high end without rich local norms
coachability_bias_risk: oral scoring subjective; output confounded with vocabulary/verbal ability and adult prompting; exposure bias present
advantage_vs_cogat: provides an ideational-fluency signal in kindergarten that CogAT does not measure; identifies creative potential before reading fluency exists
source_name: Wallach-Kogan Creativity Test - Instances (public paradigm)
reuse_note: adapt_ok - public paradigm; administer orally with a simple fluency/flexibility rubric

item_format: Similarities task: list as many ways as possible that two unlike things (e.g., an apple and an orange) are alike; scored for fluency, flexibility, originality
cognitive_process: divergent thinking / conceptual flexibility
engagement_affordance: 'connection hunter' mini-game awarding points for unexpected but valid links; streak bonuses for novel categories
adaptivity_fit: low - open-ended; scoring key required, not adaptive
tail_discrimination: med - originality and remote-association responses can flag creative talent, but reliable originality scoring is hard
coachability_bias_risk: subjective scoring; verbal-knowledge load; test-prep can inflate fluency; raters may over-credit familiar answers
advantage_vs_cogat: measures flexible/remote association central to creativity that CogAT's single-answer analogies do not reward; widens the creativity net
source_name: Wallach-Kogan Creativity Test - Similarities (public paradigm)
reuse_note: adapt_ok - public paradigm; pair with an originality key derived from local response frequencies

item_format: Pattern/Line Meanings: child views an abstract shape or line and names/draws all the things it could be; scored for fluency and originality of interpretations
cognitive_process: divergent/figural imagination
engagement_affordance: 'what could it be?' reveal game where an ambiguous doodle morphs as the child names ideas; drawing or tapping supported
adaptivity_fit: low - open figural generation; needs rubric/automated image or caption scoring
tail_discrimination: med - figural originality is a distinct talent channel, but scoring reliability limits high-tail precision
coachability_bias_risk: subjective scoring; drawing/fine-motor and verbal-labeling confounds; practice effects; rater halo toward neat drawings
advantage_vs_cogat: taps nonverbal figural creativity CogAT never scores; especially valuable for ELL and expressive-language-delayed students (equity)
source_name: Wallach-Kogan Creativity Test - Pattern/Line Meanings (public paradigm)
reuse_note: adapt_ok - public figural paradigm; useful low-language creativity channel for young/ELL learners

item_format: standardized figural creativity battery: picture construction, picture completion, and repeated-lines drawing tasks scored on fluency, originality, abstractness of titles, elaboration, and resistance to premature closure
cognitive_process: figural divergent thinking
engagement_affordance: drawing-based tasks feel like art play rather than a test; children add to and title their own pictures
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed drawing prompts scored by trained raters or a scoring service; not adaptive
tail_discrimination: med - normed figural creativity indices identify creatively gifted students, including in multicultural settings, but scoring cost/subjectivity constrain the tail
coachability_bias_risk: proprietary trained scoring reduces but does not remove subjectivity; coachable via practice; not a faking risk (performance task) but resource-intensive
advantage_vs_cogat: a normed creativity dimension CogAT lacks; widely used precisely to identify creatively gifted students that ability tests miss (equity in diverse populations)
source_name: Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT) Figural - Scholastic Testing Service
reuse_note: describe_only - commercial instrument (STS); catalog the dimensions only, do not reproduce items; license if adopted

item_format: standardized verbal creativity battery: ask-and-guess, product improvement, unusual uses, and 'just suppose' word tasks scored on fluency, flexibility, and originality
cognitive_process: verbal divergent thinking
engagement_affordance: open 'imagine if' prompts invite storytelling and playful speculation rather than right/wrong answers
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed prompts, trained/service scoring; not adaptive
tail_discrimination: med - normed verbal creativity separates creative talent but carries a high verbal-expression and scoring-reliability load
coachability_bias_risk: scoring subjective despite manuals; strong verbal/reading load (grade 1+); coachable; disadvantages ELL and reluctant writers
advantage_vs_cogat: adds a normed verbal-creativity signal absent from CogAT; identifies idea-generation talent a reasoning test cannot
source_name: Torrance Tests of Creative Thinking (TTCT) Verbal - Scholastic Testing Service
reuse_note: describe_only - commercial instrument (STS); Verbal form is grade 1-adult; describe dimensions, license before use

item_format: Consensual Assessment Technique: independent expert judges rate a child's actual creative product (story, invention, drawing) for creativity without a fixed rubric; consensus score = creativity
cognitive_process: creative production (real product)
engagement_affordance: children submit a real creation they care about (a comic, a contraption); framed as a 'maker showcase' rather than a test
adaptivity_fit: low - product-based, human expert judging; cannot be adaptive or auto-scored reliably
tail_discrimination: med-high - authentic products can reveal exceptional creativity at the tail, but depend on expert-panel availability and agreement
coachability_bias_risk: judge subjectivity and halo; product may reflect adult/home help (SES bias); resource-intensive; not fakeable like self-report, but authorship must be verified
advantage_vs_cogat: evaluates demonstrated creative output CogAT cannot elicit; captures real-world creative talent, complementing an ability score
source_name: Consensual Assessment Technique (Amabile) discussed in divergent-thinking scoring review
reuse_note: adapt_ok - method is public; requires trained judges and clear authorship/provenance rules

item_format: Academic Diligence Task: student freely allocates time between tedious-but-beneficial math practice and available distractions (games/videos); score = percent time-on-task / problems completed
cognitive_process: effort allocation / self-regulation (behavioral)
engagement_affordance: real, tempting distractions sit one tap away, making the choice to persist authentic; a progress bar rewards sustained effort
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed behavioral protocol timed across blocks; not a CAT but automatable and objectively scored
tail_discrimination: med - behaviorally separates diligent students and predicts GPA/achievement beyond IQ, though single-session estimates are noisy
coachability_bias_risk: behavioral (not self-report) so far less fakeable, but effort is state/motivation dependent and can be gamed if stakes are known; distraction appeal varies by child
advantage_vs_cogat: directly observes task commitment/diligence (Renzulli) that CogAT never measures; flags persistent under-the-radar students and de-emphasizes pure speed
source_name: Academic Diligence Task (Galla, Duckworth et al., 2014)
reuse_note: adapt_ok - published free behavioral task; re-skin distractions age-appropriately and validate locally

item_format: delay-of-gratification wait task: child can take a small reward now or wait to earn a larger one; score = wait time / choice to delay
cognitive_process: self-control / delay of gratification (behavioral)
engagement_affordance: on-screen 'treasure grows if you wait' animation with an optional 'take it now' button; the temptation is visible and real
adaptivity_fit: low - single behavioral protocol; objectively timed, not adaptive
tail_discrimination: low - wait times are highly context/trust dependent and later replications show weak, attenuated predictive validity once background is controlled
coachability_bias_risk: strongly influenced by trust in the tester and home environment (SES confound); coachable via strategies; weak long-run predictiveness (Watts et al.) - use only as a minor complementary signal
advantage_vs_cogat: observes self-regulation CogAT ignores, but its fragility is a caution: it broadens signals yet must not be over-weighted
source_name: Stanford marshmallow / delay-of-gratification paradigm (Mischel)
reuse_note: adapt_ok - public paradigm; treat cautiously given replication concerns and SES/trust confounds

item_format: behavioral persistence probe: child works on a challenging (near-unsolvable) puzzle with an easy 'stop' option always available; score = time-on-task and number of attempts before quitting
cognitive_process: persistence / effort under difficulty (behavioral)
engagement_affordance: a plucky character cheers each attempt; the child controls when to stop, so persistence is voluntary and observable
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed difficulty protocol; objectively timed, not adaptive
tail_discrimination: med - separates children who push through frustration, a key task-commitment signal, though single-task estimates are noisy
coachability_bias_risk: behavioral so less fakeable, but confounded with perceived difficulty, mood, and prior success experiences; ceiling if the puzzle seems fun rather than tedious
advantage_vs_cogat: captures grit-in-action (persisting under difficulty) that a timed reasoning test cannot see; identifies determined learners early
source_name: Behavioral persistence measures discussed in the Academic Diligence Task validation
reuse_note: adapt_ok - behavioral-persistence tradition is public; standardize difficulty and record time/attempts objectively

item_format: Short Grit Scale (Grit-S): 8 self-report statements on perseverance of effort and consistency of interest (e.g., 'I finish whatever I begin'), 5-point Likert
cognitive_process: self-perception of perseverance/passion
engagement_affordance: 'about me' slider check-in with friendly wording; only 8 items to avoid fatigue
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed short self-report scale; not adaptive and too short to bank
tail_discrimination: low - self-report ceilings and modest predictive validity (meta-analytic r is small) limit high-tail separation
coachability_bias_risk: self-report is highly fakeable and socially desirable ('I never give up'); students learn the 'right' answers; validated only from ~age 10, so 6-8 reliability is marginal
advantage_vs_cogat: names perseverance/passion (task commitment) that CogAT omits, but as self-report it is a weak, gameable signal best triangulated with behavior/teacher report
source_name: Short Grit Scale (Grit-S; Duckworth & Quinn, 2009)
reuse_note: adapt_ok - free for non-commercial research/education with attribution; do not use as a sole/primary criterion

item_format: Grit-S informant (teacher/parent) report: rater completes the 8 grit items about a specific child in third person, 5-point Likert
cognitive_process: observer rating of child perseverance
engagement_affordance: quick teacher/parent check-in embedded in a nomination workflow; 8 items keep rater burden low
adaptivity_fit: low - short fixed informant scale; not adaptive
tail_discrimination: med - observer reports of grit can outperform child self-report for young ages, but rater leniency compresses the tail
coachability_bias_risk: rater bias/halo, inconsistent standards across teachers, and inequity risk (favoring compliant or advantaged students); parents may inflate; not child-fakeable
advantage_vs_cogat: adds an observed task-commitment dimension CogAT lacks and is usable across K-8 where child self-report is unreliable; use with behavioral evidence
source_name: Short Grit Scale informant-report version (Duckworth & Quinn, 2009)
reuse_note: adapt_ok - informant form documented in the validation paper; standardize rater training to curb bias

item_format: IPIP Conscientiousness self-report items from the Self-Discipline and Achievement-Striving facets (e.g., 'I get chores done right away'), 5-point accuracy scale
cognitive_process: self-perception of conscientiousness
engagement_affordance: 'what am I like?' quiz with plain-language items and emoji anchors to hold young attention
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed Likert facet scale; not adaptive
tail_discrimination: low - self-report ceilings and social desirability blunt high-tail discrimination
coachability_bias_risk: fakeable and socially desirable; reading load; young children's self-insight is limited; acquiescence/response styles inflate scores
advantage_vs_cogat: measures conscientiousness/achievement-striving that predicts sustained achievement but is absent from CogAT; complements ability with a work-habits signal
source_name: International Personality Item Pool (IPIP) - Conscientiousness facets
reuse_note: adapt_ok - IPIP is public domain (copy/edit/translate freely); simplify wording and validate for young readers

item_format: IPIP items converted to third person so a teacher or parent rates the child's conscientiousness (e.g., 'This student gets work done right away'), 5-point scale
cognitive_process: observer rating of conscientiousness
engagement_affordance: drop-in rater form within the referral workflow; a brief facet subset keeps completion fast
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed observer scale; not adaptive
tail_discrimination: med - teacher observation of work habits is informative at the tail, but leniency and halo compress it
coachability_bias_risk: rater bias, halo from achievement, and cross-teacher inconsistency threaten equity; parents may inflate; not child-fakeable
advantage_vs_cogat: provides an observed work-habits signal across all K-8 grades that CogAT omits; useful where child self-report is unreliable
source_name: IPIP guidance on third-person (other-report) item format
reuse_note: adapt_ok - IPIP explicitly supports third-person conversion for assessments of others; standardize rater anchors

item_format: parent/teacher report of early conscientiousness/effortful control for pre-readers: adult rates observable habits (finishes tasks, follows through, resists distraction), 5-point scale
cognitive_process: observer rating of self-regulation precursors
engagement_affordance: short adult questionnaire with concrete behavior anchors ('puts toys away without reminders'); usable at kindergarten intake
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed observer scale; not adaptive
tail_discrimination: low-med - early self-regulation is developmentally noisy, so tail separation is modest
coachability_bias_risk: child self-report is invalid this young, so report-based is preferred, but rater bias/halo, SES-linked expectations, and parent inflation remain; not child-fakeable
advantage_vs_cogat: adds an early work-habits/self-regulation signal for K-1 that CogAT does not capture; report-based design avoids unreliable young self-report
source_name: IPIP third-person (other-report) conscientiousness items adapted for early grades
reuse_note: adapt_ok - use IPIP public-domain items in observer form for young children; prefer behavior anchors over trait words

item_format: IPIP curiosity/inquisitiveness self-report items (e.g., 'I love to learn new things', 'I ask a lot of questions'), 5-point accuracy scale
cognitive_process: self-perception of curiosity/intellectual engagement
engagement_affordance: 'explorer profile' builder where answers unlock a curiosity badge; plain-language items
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed Likert scale; not adaptive
tail_discrimination: low - self-report ceilings; nearly everyone endorses liking to learn, compressing the tail
coachability_bias_risk: highly fakeable/socially desirable; reading load; limited young self-insight; acquiescence bias
advantage_vs_cogat: captures curiosity/intellectual engagement (a driver of gifted development) that CogAT does not assess; complements ability with motivation-to-learn
source_name: International Personality Item Pool (IPIP) - curiosity/inquisitiveness scales
reuse_note: adapt_ok - IPIP public domain; pair self-report with a behavioral curiosity task to offset faking

item_format: uncertainty-preference behavioral curiosity task: child repeatedly chooses whether to explore certain vs uncertain options; score = threshold of desired uncertainty / exploration of the unknown
cognitive_process: information-seeking under uncertainty (behavioral)
engagement_affordance: 'mystery door vs known door' exploration game; picking the uncertain option triggers a reveal, making curiosity intrinsically fun
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed behavioral choice protocol; objectively scored, not a CAT
tail_discrimination: med - behaviorally distinguishes high-curiosity children and avoids self-report ceilings, though single-session estimates are noisy
coachability_bias_risk: behavioral (not self-report) so far less fakeable and language-light (good for ELL), but choices are state-dependent and can be shaped by prior reinforcement
advantage_vs_cogat: observes curiosity-in-action that CogAT cannot measure, and does so without reading/verbal load, broadening early identification equitably
source_name: Jirout & Klahr (2012), Children's scientific curiosity: an operational definition
reuse_note: adapt_ok - published behavioral paradigm; implement as a digital uncertainty-choice game and validate locally

item_format: epistemic-curiosity self-report (Joyous Exploration / Interest-type items adapted from the 5DCR and Epistemic Curiosity Inventory), e.g., 'I enjoy figuring out how things work', Likert
cognitive_process: self-perception of epistemic curiosity
engagement_affordance: 'what makes you wonder?' check-in with relatable scenarios; a short adapted item set
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed Likert scale; not adaptive
tail_discrimination: low-med - can separate interest-driven learners, but self-report ceilings and adult-normed wording limit the tail for children
coachability_bias_risk: fakeable/socially desirable; the original 5DCR is adult-normed (needs child adaptation/re-validation); reading load; response styles
advantage_vs_cogat: adds an epistemic-curiosity dimension (deprivation vs joyous exploration) entirely outside CogAT; flags intrinsically driven learners
source_name: Five-Dimensional Curiosity Scale-Revised (Kashdan et al.) / Epistemic Curiosity Inventory (Litman & Spielberger)
reuse_note: adapt_ok - scales described in the literature; adapt wording for children and re-validate before operational use

item_format: observed question-asking / exploration during a novel 'mystery box' activity: count and quality of information-seeking questions and exploratory actions
cognitive_process: active information seeking (behavioral)
engagement_affordance: a surprising mystery object invites 'what do you want to know?'; each question triggers a clue, rewarding inquiry
adaptivity_fit: low - observational protocol with a coding scheme; not adaptive
tail_discrimination: med - rich question-asking can flag exceptionally curious young children, but requires trained observers/coding
coachability_bias_risk: observer coding is subjective (reliability training needed); output confounded with verbal ability and comfort with adults; shy children under-produce
advantage_vs_cogat: captures spontaneous inquiry behavior CogAT never elicits; identifies inquisitive young learners regardless of test-taking skill
source_name: Jirout (2020), Supporting early scientific thinking through curiosity and question-asking
reuse_note: adapt_ok - public approach; needs a coded observation protocol and inter-rater reliability checks

item_format: Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI) Interest/Enjoyment subscale: self-report about a specific learning activity (e.g., 'I enjoyed doing this activity very much'), 7-point scale
cognitive_process: self-reported task interest/enjoyment
engagement_affordance: post-activity 'how did that feel?' reflection tied to something the child just did, increasing relevance
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed subscale referencing one activity; not adaptive
tail_discrimination: low - enjoyment ratings skew high and ceiling out, giving weak high-tail separation
coachability_bias_risk: self-report fakeable/socially desirable; ratings depend on the specific activity chosen; reading load; only Interest/Enjoyment indexes intrinsic motivation
advantage_vs_cogat: measures intrinsic interest/enjoyment that fuels gifted engagement but is invisible to CogAT; complements ability with drive-to-engage
source_name: Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI) - selfdeterminationtheory.org
reuse_note: adapt_ok - IMI freely available; use only the Interest/Enjoyment subscale as the intrinsic-motivation index and anchor it to a real task

item_format: free-choice behavioral measure: after a task's requirement ends, observe whether/how long the child keeps doing it during unstructured free time (no reward offered); score = free-choice time-on-activity
cognitive_process: intrinsic engagement (behavioral)
engagement_affordance: an open 'do whatever you like' period where the target activity remains available among alternatives; genuine choice reveals interest
adaptivity_fit: low - observational free-choice protocol; not adaptive
tail_discrimination: med - voluntary persistence at an activity is a strong intrinsic-motivation signal at the tail, though sensitive to the available alternatives
coachability_bias_risk: behavioral (not self-report) so hard to fake, but confounded by novelty and the appeal of competing options; needs unobtrusive observation to avoid demand effects
advantage_vs_cogat: observes intrinsic motivation through real behavior CogAT cannot capture; surfaces children who pursue learning for its own sake
source_name: Self-Determination Theory free-choice behavioral measure of intrinsic motivation
reuse_note: adapt_ok - classic SDT free-choice paradigm; ensure the free period is truly unrewarded and unobtrusively observed

item_format: IMI Interest/Enjoyment adapted for pre-readers: child responds to spoken items with a pictorial (smiley-face) scale about an activity they just did
cognitive_process: self-reported enjoyment (young)
engagement_affordance: tap-a-face rating right after a fun activity; no reading required
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed short adapted subscale; not adaptive
tail_discrimination: low - young faces-scale ratings are coarse and positively skewed, giving weak tail separation
coachability_bias_risk: young children acquiesce and pick the happiest face; demand characteristics from adults; self-report validity is limited at this age
advantage_vs_cogat: gives a task-interest signal for pre-readers that CogAT omits, though it should be corroborated by free-choice behavior
source_name: Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI), adapted pictorial administration - selfdeterminationtheory.org
reuse_note: adapt_ok - IMI freely available; convert to faces/oral format and treat young self-report as weak/supporting evidence

item_format: situational judgment test: child reads/hears a short social scenario and selects the most effective response option (emotion understanding/management items)
cognitive_process: applied social-emotional judgment
engagement_affordance: choose-your-response story vignettes with characters; feels like an interactive comic rather than a quiz
adaptivity_fit: med - closed-response SJT items can be banked and delivered adaptively once keyed
tail_discrimination: med - performance-based SJTs relate to ability EI more than to self-report and can discriminate judgment quality, though items are multidimensional
coachability_bias_risk: less fakeable than Likert self-report but still somewhat coachable; the scoring key can be culturally loaded; reading load; correct-response consensus can be contested
advantage_vs_cogat: assesses applied social/emotional judgment CogAT ignores and shows less adverse impact on minorities, supporting equitable identification
source_name: MacCann & Roberts SJT-based EI (STEU/STEM) validity evidence
reuse_note: adapt_ok - the SJT paradigm is public; author child-appropriate scenarios and derive a defensible scoring key

item_format: situational judgment test for task-approach/conscientiousness: 'your project is hard and boring - what do you do?' with options reflecting persistence vs avoidance
cognitive_process: applied judgment about effort/self-management
engagement_affordance: relatable school dilemmas with pickable actions and instant story consequences; supports replay for reflection
adaptivity_fit: med - keyed SJT items can be banked and adaptively administered
tail_discrimination: med - can separate mature self-management judgment, but many students recognize the 'good' answer, compressing the tail
coachability_bias_risk: partially fakeable (the socially desirable option is often guessable); reading load; multidimensional; scoring consensus needed to avoid bias
advantage_vs_cogat: probes conscientiousness/effort judgment that CogAT never measures; engaging format is less prone to faking than Likert grit items
source_name: Mosaic by ACT SEL Assessment Technical Manual (situational judgment method)
reuse_note: describe_only - Mosaic is a commercial assessment; use its public technical documentation to inform SJT design, not to copy items

item_format: animated/gamified situational judgment for young learners: an audiovisual scenario plays and the child taps the character action they think is best (curiosity/effort/prosocial choices)
cognitive_process: applied judgment (low-literacy, audiovisual)
engagement_affordance: cartoon dilemma with voice-over and tappable characters; immersive, narrative-driven, no reading needed
adaptivity_fit: med - options are closed and keyable; can be sequenced adaptively
tail_discrimination: low-med - engaging and low-literacy, but young judgment is variable and scenario realism drives validity
coachability_bias_risk: reduced faking vs self-report and low reading load (equity gain), but ecological validity hinges on scenario design; young responses are noisy; culturally sensitive keying required
advantage_vs_cogat: captures early applied judgment without reading load, a signal CogAT lacks; the audiovisual format widens access for pre-readers/ELL
source_name: OECD (2024) working paper on innovative SEL assessment (SJTs, tasks, games)
reuse_note: adapt_ok - design principles are public; build original animated scenarios and validate the scoring key with children

item_format: portfolio of student work collected over time with student reflections on each piece; reviewed against a giftedness rubric for depth, originality, and growth
cognitive_process: demonstrated achievement / self-reflection
engagement_affordance: a personal 'portfolio museum' the child curates and annotates; ownership boosts investment
adaptivity_fit: low - a qualitative body of evidence; human-rated, not adaptive or auto-scored
tail_discrimination: med-high - sustained high-quality work is a strong tail signal, but rating reliability and unequal home support limit precision
coachability_bias_risk: authorship/home-help confound (SES bias); rater subjectivity requires ~80% exact-agreement training; time-intensive; not fakeable like a Likert, but provenance matters
advantage_vs_cogat: documents demonstrated achievement and creativity over time that a one-shot CogAT cannot; NAGC-recommended for surfacing overlooked/young/ELL students
source_name: NAGC - Identification (portfolios, performances, multiple criteria)
reuse_note: describe_only - follow NAGC guidance; build a scoring rubric with trained raters and authorship safeguards

item_format: performance/authentic task scored by rubric: child designs and carries out a short investigation or open-ended product, rated on reasoning, originality, and follow-through
cognitive_process: applied problem-solving / creative production
engagement_affordance: a hands-on 'design challenge' framed as a mission; the child builds/creates rather than bubbles answers
adaptivity_fit: low - constructed performance; rubric-scored by trained raters, not adaptive
tail_discrimination: med-high - open tasks let exceptional talent show ceiling-free, but demand rigorous rater training for reliability
coachability_bias_risk: rater subjectivity (needs high exact-agreement standards); task familiarity and materials access vary by SES; coachable; authorship must be observed
advantage_vs_cogat: reveals creativity and task commitment in action, ceiling-free, unlike CogAT's fixed items; catches students who underperform on multiple-choice
source_name: KAGE / NAGC guidance on performance assessments and portfolios in identification
reuse_note: describe_only - use public performance-assessment guidance; enforce >=80% rater agreement and equitable materials

item_format: self-initiated 'passion project' showcase with a structured reflection on goals, obstacles, and persistence (Renzulli Type III style demonstrated commitment)
cognitive_process: task commitment via sustained self-directed work
engagement_affordance: the student pitches a project they chose and cares about, then reflects on how they pushed through setbacks; autonomy drives buy-in
adaptivity_fit: low - qualitative product + reflection; human-rated, not adaptive
tail_discrimination: med-high - depth and follow-through on a self-chosen project strongly signal task commitment at the tail, if authorship is genuine
coachability_bias_risk: strong SES/home-support and authorship confound; the reflection can be coached; rater subjectivity; students with fewer resources may show less polished projects
advantage_vs_cogat: captures sustained task commitment and passion (Renzulli) that CogAT structurally cannot; broadens identification to driven, project-oriented learners
source_name: NAGC - Identification (portfolios/performances with student reflection)
reuse_note: describe_only - align to NAGC multiple-criteria guidance; score process/persistence, not just polish, to reduce SES bias

item_format: structured 'tell me about what you made' interview: young child describes a self-chosen creation; scored for elaboration, originality of thinking, and evident persistence
cognitive_process: demonstrated creativity/commitment via oral account
engagement_affordance: a warm show-and-tell with a friendly interviewer; the child brings a real creation and explains it
adaptivity_fit: low - qualitative oral protocol; human-rated, not adaptive
tail_discrimination: low-med - can reveal precocious young makers, but oral accounts are noisy and heavily verbal
coachability_bias_risk: confounded with verbal ability, adult help on the creation, and comfort talking to adults (SES/ELL bias); rater subjectivity; shy children underperform
advantage_vs_cogat: gives a demonstrated-achievement/creativity signal for pre-readers that CogAT cannot, using observation over test-taking skill
source_name: NAGC - Assessments & Tests (portfolios/observations for young children)
reuse_note: describe_only - per NAGC, use observation/portfolio methods for under-6; code with a rubric and note authorship

item_format: teacher rating scale - Creativity Characteristics dimension: teacher rates observed creative behaviors (curiosity, idea generation, risk-taking, humor) on a frequency scale
cognitive_process: observer rating of creative behavior
engagement_affordance: a brief teacher checklist embedded in nomination; frequency anchors keep it fast
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed observer dimension; not adaptive
tail_discrimination: med - teacher-observed creativity adds signal, but ratings are not comparable across teachers, blurring the tail
coachability_bias_risk: rater bias/halo and cross-teacher inconsistency (a documented weakness); may under-identify nonconforming or minority students; not child-fakeable
advantage_vs_cogat: adds an observed creativity dimension grounded in Renzulli's three-ring model that CogAT omits; helps teachers surface creative talent

item_format: teacher rating scale - Motivation Characteristics dimension: teacher rates sustained absorption, persistence, and self-directed effort on tasks the student values, frequency scale
cognitive_process: observer rating of motivation/task commitment
engagement_affordance: a short teacher checklist within referral; concrete behavior anchors reduce guesswork
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed observer dimension; not adaptive
tail_discrimination: med - teacher-observed persistence is a useful tail signal but is compressed by leniency and inconsistent standards
coachability_bias_risk: rater bias/halo, cross-teacher non-comparability, and equity risk (favoring compliant students); teachers may conflate compliance with motivation; not child-fakeable
advantage_vs_cogat: operationalizes Renzulli's task-commitment ring via teacher observation - exactly the dimension CogAT structurally excludes
source_name: Renzulli Scales (SRBCSS) - Motivation Characteristics (Renzulli et al., 2010)
reuse_note: describe_only - commercial instrument; describe the Motivation dimension only; use local norms and rater training if licensed

item_format: teacher rating scale (school form) - Motivation and Creativity scales: teacher rates each behavior on a 9-point below/at/above-peer scale (12 items per scale)
cognitive_process: observer rating of motivation and creativity
engagement_affordance: a structured teacher rating tool with clear peer-referenced anchors; delivered digitally in a screening workflow
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed normed scales; not adaptive
tail_discrimination: med - normed, high-internal-consistency scales aid screening, but the Motivation/Creativity scales are weaker discriminators than the Intellectual scale
coachability_bias_risk: teacher rater bias/halo and familiarity effects; peer-referencing helps but standards still vary; girls rated slightly higher on Motivation; not child-fakeable
advantage_vs_cogat: provides normed teacher-rated Motivation and Creativity dimensions absent from CogAT; complements ability testing in a multi-criteria system

item_format: teacher rating scale (11 items) with Academic and Social/Affective components: teacher rates how often a student is an outlier vs same-age peers (e.g., 'has intense interests', 'eager to explore new concepts', 'exhibits intellectual intensity')
cognitive_process: observer rating of gifted behaviors (motivation/curiosity/affect)
engagement_affordance: a very short 11-item teacher form usable by a school committee; low burden encourages broad screening
adaptivity_fit: low - fixed short scale; not adaptive
tail_discrimination: med - designed for screening; measurement-invariant across low-income and diverse groups, which stabilizes the tail across subgroups
coachability_bias_risk: still a teacher rating (halo/leniency, cross-rater variability), but built and validated to reduce bias against low-income/culturally/linguistically diverse students; not child-fakeable
advantage_vs_cogat: adds observed motivation, curiosity, and affective giftedness that CogAT omits, and is explicitly engineered to broaden WHO gets identified (equity - core H1 advantage)
source_name: HOPE Teacher Rating Scale (Gentry, Pereira, Peters, McIntosh, Fugate, 2015); items on public FCPS screening form

item_format: 3x3 array of geometric shapes with the bottom-right cell missing; pick which of 6 options best completes the pattern
cognitive_process: inductive rule abstraction across rows and columns
engagement_affordance: 'repair the cracked mosaic' framing: the found tile snaps into the grid with a chime and the full pattern lights up, unlocking a new shape-world at higher difficulty
adaptivity_fit: high - the 11 released items map to progression/addition/distribution rules that are fully parameterizable, so Automatic Item Generation (AIG) can clone unlimited calibrated variants
tail_discrimination: high - published IRT stats show hard items (e.g. MR.50) carry peak information above +1 SD, sharpening separation near the gifted cut
coachability_bias_risk: low language/reading load makes it ELL-friendly; the public items are somewhat coachable, so operationalize AIG clones rather than the originals
advantage_vs_cogat: same nonverbal-reasoning family as CogAT Figure Matrices but items are public-domain and IRT-calibrated, giving transparent tail information and cheap fresh forms CogAT cannot supply
source_name: ICAR Matrix Reasoning (International Cognitive Ability Resource)
reuse_note: reuse_verbatim - ICAR is an explicitly public-domain measure; may reproduce or AIG-clone

item_format: Raven-like 3x3 matrix with one missing cell; select the option consistent with the relational rules running across rows and columns
cognitive_process: relational rule induction (identity, addition/subtraction, distribution of shapes)
engagement_affordance: 'pattern detective' mode where each correctly applied rule (movement, addition, subtraction) animates onto the grid, teaching the mechanic while it is scored
adaptivity_fit: high - the Sandia generator was built to systematically vary rule type and count, so difficulty is programmatically dialable for AIG item banks
tail_discrimination: high - stacking multiple simultaneous rules per matrix drives difficulty into the top tail; the 2010 norming data give ready difficulty anchors
coachability_bias_risk: low verbal load; because the generator is open we can mint novel forms that resist memorization-based coaching
advantage_vs_cogat: open, freely regenerable matrices (correlate ~.69-.93 with Raven's) give a CogAT-equivalent nonverbal signal without per-form licensing and with full control of the difficulty ladder
source_name: Sandia Matrices (Matzen et al., 2010, Behavior Research Methods)

item_format: incomplete 3x3 matrix of abstract colored shapes; identify relationships (shape, color, size, position) and choose the completing tile from distractors
cognitive_process: multi-attribute relational reasoning under time pressure
engagement_affordance: timed 'beat-your-best-streak' matrix runs with a live speed-accuracy efficiency meter, mirroring how MaRs-IB scores reasoning efficiency
adaptivity_fit: high - 80 open items span difficulty and are organized by relational structure, and the CC-BY design supports AIG expansion of the pool
tail_discrimination: high - efficiency (speed x accuracy) peaks in late adolescence, yielding a graded signal that avoids ceiling for able students
coachability_bias_risk: low language load; CC-BY openness lets us rotate item pools to blunt coaching; check color-blind accessibility of stimuli
advantage_vs_cogat: a purpose-built open alternative to copyrighted matrix tests that exposes item-level reaction-time and accuracy process data CogAT's static booklet cannot

item_format: procedurally generated 3x3 RPM-style matrix with structured rules (constant, progression, arithmetic, distribute-three) across attributes; pick the missing panel from 8 options
cognitive_process: hierarchical relational and analogical reasoning
engagement_affordance: an endless procedurally-generated 'matrix dungeon' where each floor introduces a new rule family; because items are machine-generated, no two runs repeat
adaptivity_fit: high - the attributed stochastic image grammar generates unlimited matrices with labeled rule structures, the archetype of rule-parameterized AIG
tail_discrimination: high - number and compositionality of rules is a direct difficulty knob, enabling items calibrated specifically for the top percentile
coachability_bias_risk: low language load; effectively uncoachable because every form is freshly generated
advantage_vs_cogat: an inexhaustible, structure-labeled matrix supply with known generative rules, so the tail can be targeted and forms refreshed in ways CogAT's fixed proprietary items cannot

item_format: procedurally generated matrix where relations (progression, XOR, OR, AND, consistent union) act on attributes (size, color, position, number); choose the panel completing the set
cognitive_process: abstract relational reasoning with generalization across rule regimes
engagement_affordance: a 'rule lab' where solving reveals which hidden relation (XOR, AND, progression) governed the grid, turning each item into a mini experiment
adaptivity_fit: high - relation x object x attribute triples are explicit generator parameters, the definition of rule-parameterized AIG at scale (1.4M items)
tail_discrimination: high - logical relations (XOR/AND) and multi-triple structures create very hard items that discriminate the extreme tail
coachability_bias_risk: low verbal load; infinite generation defeats item-exposure coaching
advantage_vs_cogat: supports held-out generalization regimes, so we can measure genuine rule transfer (not memorized templates), a fairness and robustness edge over CogAT's fixed forms

item_format: matrix-completion items produced from a cognitive model that sets number of rules, abstraction level, and perceptual features to hit a target difficulty (method described, not a fixed item)

coachability_bias_risk: low language load; model-generated novelty limits coaching; document rule-type practice effects

tail_discrimination: med - a single dominant relation per 2x2 limits top-end stretch versus multi-rule 3x3 matrices
coachability_bias_risk: high - one of the most heavily test-prepped gifted formats; secure items cannot be refreshed by us
advantage_vs_cogat: documents the incumbent we must beat: describing (not copying) it shows where AIG 3x3 matrices add tail information and coaching resistance
